raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable bioelectronic therapy for patients with symptomatic heart failure (HF), particularly those with reduced or mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), narrow QRS complexes, and no indication for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT). CCM delivers relatively high-voltage, biphasic electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period, thereby avoiding myocardial depolarization while modulating contractile performance [1,2]. This distinguishes CCM from pacing and CRT: it is not intended to resynchronize activation, but to improve myocardial calcium handling, contractile protein function, autonomic balance, and reverse-remodeling pathways [20-24].

Early human studies established feasibility and acute hemodynamic effects in advanced HF with normal QRS duration [1]. The randomized, double-blind FIX-CHF-4 crossover trial subsequently showed improvements in peak oxygen consumption and quality of life, though with important placebo and crossover considerations [2]. The larger FIX-HF-5 program broadened evaluation in patients with NYHA class III–IV symptoms and reduced LVEF [3,4]. Although the overall FIX-HF-5 trial did not meet its primary ventilatory anaerobic threshold endpoint, prespecified analyses suggested greater benefit in patients with LVEF 25%–45%, a population later targeted prospectively [5,6].

The pivotal FIX-HF-5C study randomized symptomatic patients with LVEF 25%–45% and QRS duration <130 ms to CCM plus medical therapy versus medical therapy alone. CCM improved peak VO₂, 6-minute walk distance, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire score, and NYHA class, and suggested fewer cardiovascular death/HF hospitalization events [7]. The 2-lead Optimizer Smart system was then evaluated in FIX-HF-5C2, demonstrating acceptable device safety and performance while simplifying implantation by eliminating the atrial lead [8]. These data underpin current clinical use in carefully selected patients who remain symptomatic despite guideline-directed medical therapy and who are not CRT candidates.

Observational studies have extended CCM experience to clinically relevant subgroups. Patients with permanent atrial fibrillation appear feasible candidates, particularly with newer 2-lead systems [9]. CCM has also been used in CRT nonresponders, though evidence is limited and such use should be individualized [10]. Case reports describe dramatic reverse remodeling or “super-response,” but these should be viewed as hypothesis-generating [11]. Longer-term single-center and multicenter registries suggest sustained improvements in NYHA class, quality of life, LVEF, and hospitalization rates, with survival sometimes better than predicted by risk models [12-16]. However, these comparisons are vulnerable to selection bias, regression to the mean, and confounding by concurrent medical optimization.

Meta-analyses generally support a consistent symptomatic signal. Earlier randomized-trial syntheses found improvement in quality-of-life measures, with less certain effects on 6-minute walk distance, hospitalization, arrhythmias, or mortality [17,18]. More recent analyses incorporating observational cohorts report favorable changes in functional status and remodeling, but confirm that definitive mortality benefit has not been established [19]. Thus, CCM should be considered an adjunctive therapy aimed primarily at symptoms, exercise capacity, and health status rather than a proven disease-modifying substitute for foundational HF therapies.

Mechanistically, CCM appears to normalize aspects of maladaptive HF biology rather than simply provide acute inotropy. Translational work summarized in contemporary reviews suggests improved sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium cycling, SERCA2a/phospholamban regulation, reversal of fetal gene expression, reduced fibrosis signaling, and improved energetic efficiency without the oxygen-cost profile typical of pharmacologic inotropes [20-24]. These mechanisms may explain why benefits can extend beyond the immediate stimulation site and persist over months.

Patient selection remains central. The strongest evidence supports patients with persistent NYHA class III symptoms, LVEF approximately 25%–45%, sinus rhythm or controlled atrial arrhythmias, narrow QRS complexes, optimized medical therapy, and no CRT indication [7,8,20,23]. Practical issues include venous access, lead placement, interaction testing in patients with ICDs, infection risk, tricuspid valve considerations, and the need for regular device charging and follow-up [22,26,27]. Data in HFpEF, transplant recipients, and unusual cardiomyopathies remain preliminary [25,30].

In summary, CCM fills an important therapeutic niche for symptomatic HF patients who remain limited despite contemporary pharmacologic and device therapy but lack a CRT target. The evidence base is strongest for improvements in exercise tolerance, quality of life, and functional class; registry data are encouraging for hospitalization reduction, but randomized outcome trials with adequate power and modern background therapy are still needed. Ongoing work should refine mechanistic biomarkers, identify responders, integrate CCM with ICD-capable platforms, and clarify its role across the LVEF spectrum [24,28,29].
